key_insight: RL-trained LLM agents can learn to call tools for the wrong reason—reacting to superficial cues instead of actual task need—especially after they become competent at using the tool.
engineering_relevance: For reliable agentic systems, tool-use training should reward necessity and robustness, not just success, to avoid brittle, cue-driven behavior in math and QA workflows.
method: Built controlled synthetic QA and math environments with cue-to-tool correlations that are causally irrelevant.
Ran counterfactual evaluations where cues remained but tool necessity changed.
Added a dense, decision-level LLM-judge reward to score whether each tool call was actually needed.
evidence_signal: Across counterfactual tests, spurious tool invocation rose by up to 39%, and shortcut behavior appeared only after the agent had learned the target tool reliably.
watch_item: An LLM-judge reward can reduce shortcut behavior, but its own judgments must be calibrated carefully to avoid introducing new bias or reward noise.
paper_title: Spurious Tool Use: When RL Agents Learn the Wrong Reason to Act
